Unlocking Educational Ethos: Why It Truly Matters in Schools
Understanding educational ethos: why it matters in schools
When considering a school for your child, you might ask: What is ethos in schools, and why is it important? Educational ethos refers to the core values, beliefs, and principles that shape a school’s culture, teaching methods, and overall environment. It’s the invisible thread that ties together curriculum, behaviour, and community, influencing how students learn, interact, and grow.
A strong educational ethos fosters a positive learning atmosphere, promotes respect and inclusivity, and aligns academic goals with personal development. It’s not just about what students learn, but how they learn and who they become in the process.
The Lyceum School: A Model of Purposeful Education
At The Lyceum School in the City of London, the educational ethos is deeply embedded in its mission and daily practices. Founded in 1997 by Lynn Hannay and Jeremy Rowe, the school was established with a thematic and flexible teaching model aimed at infusing creativity into academic success. This foundational ethos continues to guide the school’s approach to education.
Vision and Aims
The Lyceum’s vision is to provide an education for children that prepares them for today, tomorrow, and the future. Their aims include:
Developing a deep love of learning: Inspiring students through an exciting, topic-based curriculum that uses London as a classroom.
Challenging the status quo: Encouraging critical thinking and problem-solving, particularly through STEAM education.
Seeing every day as an adventure: Promoting a risk-taking and adventurous approach to learning.
Creating an environment full of laughter and happiness: Ensuring every child feels valued, listened to, and celebrated.
Fostering kindness, confidence, and creativity: Preparing students to be resilient, entrepreneurial, and philanthropic.
Building a community: Embracing a diverse and multicultural environment that reflects 21st-century London.
Creating treasured moments: Partnering with parents to involve them in school activities and celebrations.
The Four Pillars of The Lyceum
Central to The Lyceum’s ethos are its four pillars:
These pillars are not just abstract concepts, they are integrated into everyday learning and serve as visual reminders within the school, reinforcing the values that guide student behaviour and interactions.
Kindness: Cultivating empathy and compassion among students.
Creativity: Encouraging innovative thinking and expression.
Confidence: Building self-assurance and resilience.
Pastoral Care and Personal Development
The Lyceum places a strong emphasis on pastoral care, recognising the importance of spiritual, moral, social, and cultural development. Initiatives like the School and Eco Councils involve students in decision-making processes, promoting self-knowledge, self-respect, and critical thinking skills.
Programs such as ‘Tea and Toast’ provide Year 6 pupils with opportunities to discuss emotions, manage stress, and develop life skills, preparing them for challenges beyond the classroom.
Ethos in Action
The Lyceum’s commitment to its ethos is evident in its daily operations and interactions. From the curriculum design to extracurricular activities, every aspect of the school reflects its core values. The integration of kindness, creativity, confidence, and community into the fabric of school life ensures that students not only excel academically but also grow into well-rounded individuals ready to contribute positively to society.
About The Lyceum School
The Lyceum School is a place where every child is cherished, known, and celebrated. Situated in the vibrant heart of the City of London, our school offers a nurturing, co-educational environment founded on the pillars of kindness, creativity, confidence, and community. We inspire a deep love of learning through an engaging, topic-based curriculum using London as our classroom, enriched by STEAM, language, arts, and wellbeing-focused initiatives like mindfulness and yoga.
With small class sizes, high staff-to-pupil ratios, and a strong pastoral framework, including our House System and accessible pastoral support, we prioritise each child’s personal growth just as much as academic success.
Located near Old Street, Liverpool Street, Moorgate and Shoreditch stations, our modern, light-filled five-storey building with specialist art, science, STEAM studios and outdoor space provides a dynamic setting that’s seamlessly integrated with London’s rich cultural resources. At The Lyceum, learning comes alive every day, preparing children to become confident, compassionate, and curious individuals ready to contribute positively to the world.
Attend Our Open Day
Curious about life at The Lyceum? Come see it for yourself. Join one of our Open Days to explore our modern building, meet our lovely staff and feel the energy of our school community. You’ll get a real sense of what makes our independent co-ed school so special.
Can’t make it to an Open Day? No problem. Just contact our team to book a private tour.
📧 Email: registrar@lyceumschool.co.uk 📞 Phone: +44 (0)20 7247 1588
Final thoughts
In conclusion, the educational ethos of a school like The Lyceum is more than a set of ideals; it’s a living, breathing part of the school’s identity that shapes every student’s experience. By prioritising values such as kindness, creativity, confidence, and community, The Lyceum demonstrates how a strong ethos can lead to a nurturing, dynamic, and effective learning environment.

Vision & Aims
Our Vision, Aims & Ethos
Every school has a character of its own: the beliefs and values that shape how children are taught, how they are cared for and how they treat one another. At The Lyceum, our educational ethos is simple to state and lived out every day. We want every child to be happy, to love learning and to grow into a kind, confident and creative young person who makes a positive contribution to the world.
What Is a School’s Ethos?
An ethos is the set of guiding beliefs and values that give a community its character. A school’s ethos describes what it believes education is for and how those beliefs shape daily life, from lessons and relationships to behaviour, wellbeing and the way the school works with families. When you visit a school, its ethos is what you feel: the atmosphere in the corridors, the way children speak to adults and the way staff speak about children.
Our Vision
“To provide an education for children, for today, tomorrow and the future.”
When Lynn Hannay and Jeremy Rowe founded The Lyceum in 1997, they set out to infuse creativity into academic success through a thematic and flexible approach to teaching. More than 25 years later, that vision remains at the heart of our school. We prepare children for the next stage of their education, and also for a fast-changing world that will need resilient, creative and compassionate people.
Our Aims
Our aims guide every decision we make, from the design of our curriculum to the way we celebrate each child.
Our Four Pillars
Our ethos of education rests on four core values, which we call our four pillars. They are literally built into the school: structural pillars throughout our building are dedicated to each value, as daily reminders for everyone who passes them.
What it means at The Lyceum
Treating everyone with respect and care, and embedding kindness in daily routines from Reception onwards
Imagining, making and experimenting across the arts, STEAM and every subject
Having the self-belief to speak up, take on challenges and keep trying
Belonging to a close, diverse school family and contributing to the wider world
Our Ethos in Action
An ethos only matters if you can see it in daily school life. At The Lyceum, you’ll find it in:
Our December 2025 ISI inspection feedback reflected this culture, noting that “the school culture directly and positively impacts the pupils’ development” and that The Lyceum “recognises individual differences and promotes the tolerance of others.”
Discover The Lyceum for Yourself
The best way to understand a school’s ethos is to experience it. We warmly invite you to visit us, read a welcome from our Headmaster, or learn more about us and our co-educational approach.
Explore Admissions →
Frequently Asked Questions
What is The Lyceum School's educational ethos?
Our ethos is built on four pillars: kindness, creativity, confidence and community. We believe children learn best when they are happy, feel valued and are inspired by exciting learning. We combine academic ambition with creativity, using London as our classroom, so that every pupil leaves The Lyceum with a lifelong love of learning and the confidence to make a positive contribution to the world.
Why does a school's ethos matter when choosing a school?
A school’s ethos shapes your child’s everyday experience: how they are taught, how they are supported when things are difficult and how they learn to treat others. Two schools with similar results can feel very different. Understanding a school’s ethos, and seeing it in action on a visit, helps you choose a place where your child will be happy and able to thrive.
How can I see The Lyceum's ethos in action?
The best way is to visit. At our Open Mornings, you can meet our Headmaster, see lessons in progress and talk to pupils, who are always our best ambassadors. You’re also welcome to arrange a private visit at a time that suits you. Email registrar@lyceumschool.co.uk or call 020 7247 1588 to book.

In 2019 we moved into our current building on Worship street after many years at a site just round the corner at Paul Street.

Welcome from the Headmaster
Welcome
It gives me great pleasure to welcome you to The Lyceum, a unique co-educational day school for children aged 4 – 11-years old in the heart of the City of London.
I am sure that every Head says this about their school, but The Lyceum truly is a magical place.
Everyone who visits remarks on the palpable energy, happiness and how confident, kind, creative and community-minded our pupils are.
What they feel are the magic ingredients that bring our school to life – they see how:
Our children develop a deep love of learning
We inspire a love of learning through our exciting, topic-based curriculum where we use London as our classroom.
We challenge the status quo
Our children think critically, and problem solve, especially through our STEAM education.
Our children see every day as an adventure
We encourage a risk-taking and adventurous approach where exciting learning happens every day.
Our school is full of laughter and happiness
Every child is valued, listened to, and celebrated.
Our children are kind, confident, and creative
We prepare them to be resilient, entrepreneurial and philanthropic equipped with a set of skills to make a positive contribution to the world.
We take pride in our diverse and multi-cultural community; a true reflection of 21st century London.
We create treasured moments
We don’t want our busy working parents to miss out. We work in strong partnership with parents, inviting them to join us for assemblies, workshops and enjoy lunch with their children.
Pupil Wellbeing
Nothing is more important than your child, and we do all we can to prepare them for life today, tomorrow and the future.
Through our small class sizes, our staff team form strong connections with our pupils and our house system encourages community building and facilitates peer-to-peer support and encouragement. These are fundamental relationships that help our pupils thrive and understand who they are.
We understand today’s complicated world for children and help our young people develop their inner strength to be able to thrive in it. Through an interwoven PSHE curriculum and mindfulness approach, we provide them with a toolkit to support their physical, emotional, and mental wellbeing. We teach them how to eat healthily, stay balanced and regulate their emotions through breathing exercises, yoga and reflection time.
Academic results are important – and our pupils go on to achieve stellar results at the 11+ – but we prioritise their happiness. This preparation puts them in good stead not just for their next step into senior school, but for their entire adult lives.
Embracing a STEAM curriculum
Many of the jobs our pupils will have do not yet exist. Preparing them for this world begins as early as Reception and our topic-based curriculum centres on Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Mathematics (STEAM).
Our new technology hub allows our children opportunities to be creative, innovative and prepared for life in the 21st century.
We are a school for busy, professional parents
Our location is perfect for those who work or live in the City, and our wrap-around care gives you peace of mind from 8am-5:45pm each day.
Breakfast club starts at 8am and from 3:45pm we offer an extensive range of after school clubs offering everything from creative arts and coding, to sing and sign and fencing.
As busy parents we also don’t want you to miss out, so regularly invite you to join us during assemblies, for lunch and during themed weeks at school.
We would love to welcome you to our community
We know our children’s days here at ones they will remember for their rest of their lives; every day is an adventure, filled with fun and laughter alongside academic excellence.
You are warmly invited to come visit and see our wonderful school in action.

Independent Prep School in Shoreditch
Shoreditch might be better known for start-ups and street art than for schools, yet behind our big black carriage doors is The Lyceum School, a co-educational independent prep school for children aged 4 to 11.
Since 1997, we have called East London our home and given families from across the City of London, Hackney, and Islington a chance at a truly transformational private education. Using the city as a classroom, our pupils get front-row seats to one of the world’s most culturally significant centres, with frequent trips to museums, parks and theatres – as well as our fantastic modern school building with specialist Art, Science and STEAM studios.
Where We Are Located
The Lyceum School is at 65 Worship Street, London EC2A 2DU, an independent school in Shoreditch, just beside the City of London. Our five-storey former print works has been transformed into bright classrooms, a library, a hall, a dining room with a mural of the London skyline and The Owlery, our STEAM Studio. An astroturf playground with colourful murals gives children space to play every day. It makes us a genuinely central private school: Shoreditch, the City and Hoxton are all on our doorstep.
Our partner nursery, Hopes and Dreams Montessori Nursery, is in the same building, so the youngest children can move to Reception without changing address. For sport and performances, we make the most of the neighbourhood, using Shoreditch Power League, Mile End Stadium, York Hall and St Giles Cripplegate throughout the year.
Areas We Serve
Families come to The Lyceum School from across Islington, Hackney and Camden, as well as the City of London, Shoreditch, Hoxton, Clerkenwell and Tower Hamlets. Many parents work in the City, so a school a short walk from Liverpool Street and Moorgate makes the daily routine far simpler.
For families looking for a private school near Islington, we are one stop from Angel on the Northern line to Old Street. As one of the independent schools in Hackney, we are a short Overground ride from Dalston, Haggerston and Hoxton. East London families based in Tower Hamlets, from Bethnal Green to Stratford, can reach us on the Central line to Liverpool Street.
Whether you are comparing the best private schools in central London or looking for a prep school in the City of London close to your office, our location makes the school run easy.
Getting to The Lyceum School
Most of our children walk, scoot or cycle to school, and we encourage families to use public transport. As one of the prep schools near Old Street and Liverpool Street, we are well connected to the Underground, Elizabeth line, Overground and National Rail.
Liverpool Street Station (Central, Circle, Hammersmith & City and Metropolitan Line)
Old Street Station (Northern Line)
Moorgate Station (Elizabeth and Northern Line)
Liverpool Street Station (Weaver Line)
Shoreditch High Street Station (Weaver Line)
Liverpool Street Station (Greater Anglia, Stansted Express, C2C)
Old Street Station (Great Northern)
Routes 21, 43, 76, 141 at Epworth Street
Routes 8, 26, 35, 42, 47, 78, 135, 149, 388 at Primrose Street
On-street parking around Worship Street is limited because of the local controlled parking zone, and the area falls within the central London Congestion Charge zone. We recommend walking, cycling or public transport wherever possible.
Local Area and Community
Our neighbourhood is one of London’s most exciting, and we use it every week. Finsbury Square and Bunhill Fields are moments away, and our choirs perform at Wesley’s Chapel on City Road and in the Broadgate Quarter by Liverpool Street.
For families looking for schools near Spitalfields or Bishopsgate, we are a short walk away. Spitalfields Market, Hoxton Square, Shoreditch Park, and Columbia Road Flower Market bring history, art, and culture to our doorstep. The Barbican and St Giles Cripplegate host our summer musical, while trips to museums and galleries across the capital bring our topic-based curriculum to life.
We also give back to the community. Pupils collect for Hackney Food Bank each term, lead half-termly litter picks and perform for residents of local care homes, part of the work that earned us an Eco-Schools Green Flag with Distinction in 2024.
A Shared History: The Lyceum School and the Dukes Family
Two teachers from the state sector founded The Lyceum School to create a small, creative school where children would love learning. From the beginning, the school combined a strong foundation in the National Curriculum with cross-curricular topic work.
When the school moved into its current home on Worship Street, parents and children were asked which words came to mind when they thought of The Lyceum School. The four most common answers, Kindness, Confidence, Creativity and Community, became the pillars that guide us today.
Today, The Lyceum School is part of Dukes Education, a family of independent schools, nurseries and colleges. Being part of the Dukes Education Family allows Little Dukes nurseries, like Hopes and Dreams Montessori, to benefit from a guaranteed entry policy, meaning that when children are ready for Reception, their place in a Dukes prep school is assured.
Partner Nursery and Prep School in Shoreditch
Children can begin their journey at our partner nursery, Hopes and Dreams Montessori Nursery, which has cared for local families for 24 years and welcomes children from 3 months to 5 years, with wraparound care from 8 am to 6 pm year-round. Children who enter Hopes and Dreams are given priority entry into our Reception and Prep School.
At 11, our pupils move on to leading senior schools. In 2025 – 2026, 93% of our pupils received offers from their first-choice senior schools. Recent offers include:
Highgate
Forest School
Francis Holland Regent’s Park
Queen’s College
North London Collegiate School.

Frequently Asked Questions About The Lyceum School’s Location
Where is The Lyceum School located?
The Lyceum School is at 65 Worship Street, London EC2A 2DU, on the border of Shoreditch and the City of London. We are a short walk from Old Street, Liverpool Street, Moorgate, and Shoreditch High Street stations, making us a convenient prep school in EC2A for families who live or work in central and East London.
Which areas does The Lyceum School serve?
We are a central London private school for families in East London, North London, and the City. Families tend to join us from Islington, Hackney, Camden, the City of London, Shoreditch, Hoxton, Clerkenwell and Tower Hamlets. Many parents choose The Lyceum School because it is close to their workplace in the City, and good transport links mean children can travel easily from further afield in North and East London.
Is The Lyceum School a private school for Islington families?
Yes. Although we are in Shoreditch rather than Islington, many of our families live there. For families looking for a private school, Islington is close by: Old Street is one stop from Angel on the Northern line, so we are a prep school Islington families can reach in minutes. Our partner nursery, Hopes and Dreams, also has a setting at Angel.
Is The Lyceum School in Hackney or the City of London?
Our home borough is Hackney. For parents searching for a private school, Hackney and the City are both on our doorstep: The Lyceum School sits in the London Borough of Hackney, just outside the City of London boundary, with an EC2A postcode. That makes us a local prep school in Hackney, just minutes from the Square Mile. Many families think of us as a City school, and our neighbours in the City are just a few minutes’ walk away.
How do I get to The Lyceum School by public transport?
The nearest stations are Old Street (Northern line), Liverpool Street (Central, Circle, Hammersmith & City, Metropolitan and Elizabeth lines), Moorgate and Shoreditch High Street (London Overground). Buses along City Road, Old Street and Shoreditch High Street also stop nearby.
Is there parking at The Lyceum School?
On-street parking near Worship Street is limited by the local controlled parking zone. Most of our families walk, scoot, cycle or use public transport, and we actively encourage sustainable travel as part of our commitment to the environment.
Is The Lyceum School connected to other schools called Lyceum?
No. The Lyceum School in Shoreditch, London, is an independent co-educational prep school for children aged 4 to 11 and part of Dukes Education. It is not connected to other schools, theatres or organisations that share the Lyceum name in the UK or overseas.
What is The Lyceum School’s connection to Dukes Education and Hopes and Dreams?
The Lyceum School is part of Dukes Education, a family of independent schools and nurseries. Our partner, Hopes and Dreams Montessori Nursery, is also part of the Dukes family and is based in our Worship Street building. Children at the nursery benefit from priority entry to our Reception class, shared assemblies, story time and joint trips.
What age range does The Lyceum School accept?
The Lyceum School welcomes children from age 4 in Reception through to Year 6 (age 11). Younger children can attend our partner nursery, Hopes and Dreams Montessori Nursery, in the same building from age 3. Entry to Reception is non-selective, while children joining Years 2 to 6 take a short assessment in English and Maths.
Is The Lyceum School suitable for working families or families relocating to London?
Yes. Our central location near Liverpool Street and Moorgate, along with wrap-around care from 8am to 5.45pm, makes The Lyceum School a natural choice for working families and those relocating to London. We welcome children joining mid-year where places allow, and we support pupils who speak English as an additional language.

pageCache.pageTitle: Inspiring Music Education | The Lyceum School
pageCache.text:
Music
Music at The Lyceum
Music fills our school every day. At The Lyceum, we believe music is vital for both mental and physical wellbeing, and it is an integral part of daily life at our London prep school. From Reception children singing in class to Year 6 pupils performing with our Big Band, every child is encouraged to discover the joy of making music, and many go on to achieve remarkable things.
Music for Every Child
Every pupil from Reception to Year 6 receives weekly class music lessons from our specialist music teacher. Children learn to sing, play, listen, compose and perform. They explore rhythm, pitch and notation, and they discover music from a wide range of cultures, traditions and periods. Musical learning often links to class topics. British Sign Language is often built into our choir performances, which makes music inclusive and expressive for everyone.
Music begins in the Early Years. In Reception, children sing regularly, explore percussion and move to music. For those who want more, our after-school Music Club and Sing & Sign club are open to Reception children.
Instrumental and Vocal Lessons
Our team of 13 visiting specialist music teachers offers individual and small-group lessons during the school day on 18 instruments, as well as singing lessons:
Violin, viola, cello, double bass, guitar, ukulele
Recorder, flute, clarinet, oboe, bassoon, saxophone
Trumpet, trombone, French horn
Percussion and voice
Lessons are open to pupils from Reception onwards, and instrumental pupils are encouraged to join an ensemble as soon as they are ready. Details of lesson charges can be found on our Fees page.
Choirs and Ensembles
Making music together builds friendship, teamwork and confidence. Our ensembles include:
The Big Band
The School Orchestra
Performances Throughout the Year
Performing is a big part of musical life at The Lyceum. Pupils perform in class assemblies, concerts, carol services and local festivals. Every pupil from Year 3 upwards takes part in a musical production. Each summer, pupils from Years 1 to 6 perform in our musical extravaganza at St Giles Cripplegate in the Barbican, one of the highlights of our year.
Music also connects us with our local community. Our choirs have sung for residents of a local care home and performed at community venues across the City.
Music Scholarships and Beyond
Many of our pupils continue their musical journeys at senior school, and some with great distinction. In 2025–26, Lyceum leavers won six music scholarships, at Farrington’s, Forest School, Francis Holland Regent’s Park, Highgate, Queen’s College and UCS. In 2024–25, two of our pupils gained places at specialist music schools, The Purcell School and Yehudi Menuhin School, each with a music scholarship.
Whether your child dreams of a music scholarship or simply loves to sing, our teachers will help them grow as musicians and as performers.
Why Music Matters
Learning music develops concentration, memory, coordination and perseverance, as well as creativity and self-expression. Performing builds confidence, and playing in an ensemble teaches children to listen and work as a team. The government’s National Plan for Music Education highlights the importance of every child having the chance to sing, play an instrument and perform. At The Lyceum, that opportunity is part of every child’s school day.
Explore more of our creative curriculum, including art, STEAM and our extracurricular clubs, such as Music Club, Sing & Sign and Boogie Beats.

Anmol Mohara - Drums
Anmol Mohara is a freelance drummer originally from Nepal but based in London. Anmol was the “UK Young Drummer Of The Year 2017” and “Yamaha Future Beat 2018” winner. He has played with variety of people and bands such as Nicolas Meier, Antoine Fafard, Nepalese Folk Symphony Orchestra, Ben Waters, Phil Meadows, Gareth Lockrane, Loz Speyer, Leoni Jane Kennedy and many more. Anmol has performed at the U.K Drum Show 2017 and the London Drum Show 2018 along with other various well-established venues in Nepal and the UK. Anmol graduated from the prestigious Guildhall School Of Music & Drama in 2023 where he studied jazz drums. Anmol also plays Tabla and Nepali folk percussion instruments.
Caoimhe de Paor - Recorder
Having graduated top of her class from the Cork School of Music (B.Mus), Caoimhe moved to London, where she gained a distinction in her Masters in Performance from the Guildhall School of Music and Drama. She was also awarded the school’s Concert Recital Diploma (for outstanding recital performance). Caoimhe went on to become an Artist Fellow at the conservatoire and was also invited to take part in the Handel House Talent Scheme (2014-15).
She has studied with Ian Wilson, Robert Ehrlich, Pamela Thorby (GSMD) and Elizabeth Jones (CSM), as well as pariticipating in masterclasses with Kees Boeke, Karl van Steenhoven, Piers Adams, Sebastien Marq, Dan Laurin, Drora Bruck and Eric Bosgraaf.
Caoimhe has achieved a number of competition successes in Ireland and the UK. She was a semi-finalist in the Irish Freemason’s Young Musician of the Year for two consecutive years, a finalist in the Worshipful Company of Needlemaker’s competition, a finalist in the Yamaha Music Foundation of Europe Scholarships and won first prize in the Recorder Conservatoire competition at the North London Festival of Music.
Caoimhe has performed as a chamber musician and soloist in prominent events and venues, including Wigmore Hall (Chamber Tots series), Wilton’s Music Hall, Handel and Hendrix Museum, Crypt of Mont St. Michel, Royal Greenwich International Early Music Festival, East Cork Early Music Festival, St. Barrahane’s Festival of Music, Tel-Aviv Early Music Seminar (Israel), World Forum on Music (Brisbane) and London Handel Festival. Most recently, she has given the Irish premiere of Richard Harvey’s Concerto Incantato with the UL orchestra, recorded for The New York Times Conception series, performed live on BBC Radio 3 ‘In Tune’ with her quartet Palisander, and is a member of the opera chamber ensemble, Insieme, an Ensemble-in-Residence at Lauderdale House in London.

Nicholas Ellis - Woodwind and Piano
Nick has held teaching positions (clarinet, flute and saxophone) at the Lyceum School, More House School and acted as a deputy at King’s College School Wimbledon, Sussex House Boys and Frances Holland School.

As a chamber musician Nicholas won first prize in the Royal Overseas League Chamber Music Competition with his acclaimed quintet, Camarilla Ensemble and has since performed a number of times at the Wigmore Hall, the Queen Elizabeth Hall and at Edinburgh Festival. When performing solo, Ali is particularly interested in building the classical guitar repertoire with new compositions that combine influences from Middle-Eastern and Western traditions.

What is an extra curricular activity?
Beyond the classroom walls, extra curricular activities are where much of the magic happens. These are clubs, sports, arts and enrichment opportunities that run before or after regular school hours. They give children the chance to try new things, discover hidden interests, make friends across different years, and build confidence.
From problem solving to teamwork, creativity to resilience, these activities help children develop skills that support not just their academic journey but their character too. Participating in a drama club might help a shy child find their voice. Learning a musical instrument builds discipline and patience. Team sports teach cooperation, while art or coding clubs foster innovation and independent thinking. Cognitive benefits include improved concentration, better memory, greater flexibility of thought, and boosted motivation to learn.

A comprehensive guide to the reception curriculum at The Lyceum School
Curriculum for reception in the UK
Choosing the right school for your child often comes with many questions, especially about the reception curriculum. Parents commonly ask: What does a Reception class curriculum look like? How is learning structured for young children? How do schools balance play and academic development? Reception is a crucial stage in a child’s education, forming part of the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) and laying the foundation for literacy, numeracy, social skills, and emotional wellbeing. A well-designed Reception curriculum nurtures curiosity, confidence, and independence while ensuring children feel happy and safe in their first school environment.
At The Lyceum School, the Reception class curriculum is designed with these priorities in mind. The school combines structured learning with play-based exploration, enriching experiences, and a strong focus on personal development, providing children with a smooth and engaging start to school life.
Key areas of learning in reception
The Reception curriculum at The Lyceum covers seven core areas:
Mathematics: Exploring numbers, shapes, measurement, and problem-solving.
First Days: a smooth transition
Teaching staff greet pupils and parents at drop-off every day, creating a welcoming start to the school day. This allows any messages from home to be shared directly with the team. Collection time at the end of the day also gives parents a chance to catch up with staff, or to arrange a ‘touch base’ meeting if more time is needed. Starting school can be an emotional experience for both children and parents, and the team at The Lyceum is always on hand to provide reassurance and comfort.
Very quickly, most pupil settle happily into new routines. Reception children are encouraged to develop independence from the start. They learn to carry their own bags, unpack, hang coats and hats, remember what to bring each day, and understand when to wear their PE kit or full uniform.
Child-initiated play
Play-based education lies at the heart of the Reception curriculum. Children learn key skills naturally through imaginative and creative lessons, without feeling pressure. At The Lyceum, the distinction between play and learning is blurred, making education enjoyable and fostering a lifelong love of learning.
Reception pupils follow a slightly more structured day than in Nursery. Mornings include three lessons, with a play/snack break after the first. After lunch and outdoor play, afternoons feature topic-based lessons, structured play, or park visits. The curriculum is further enriched with weekly Spanish, music, PE/dance, and yoga lessons. The dedicated team tailors learning to each child’s interests and needs. Pupils are not formally grouped or labelled, but the curriculum is subtly differentiated to challenge them appropriately.
Literacy in reception
Literacy, or Phonics, is a key part of the Reception curriculum. Phonics is a systematic approach to early reading, teaching children to match letters with their corresponding sounds. Children begin with the most common sounds of letters and progress to combining letters to form short words. Digraphs and trigraphs, where two or three letters make a new sound, are introduced once pupils are ready.
Pupils are encouraged to write using the sounds they know. Tricky words, which are not phonetic, are taught separately to ensure children can access reading materials and use them in writing. Workshops for parents in Phonics, early Maths, and Parenting are offered, and staff provide regular guidance to support children’s learning at home.
Numeracy
Mathematics is taught in a fun and engaging way. By the end of Reception, pupils can explain their reasoning as well as find answers. Learning progresses from number recognition to addition, subtraction, doubling, halving, and problem-solving. Shape, position, movement, time, and measurement are also explored, embedding correct mathematical language and preparing pupils for “Singapore Maths No Problem” in Year One.
Mealtimes
Snack and lunch are supervised by the EYFS team. Pupils eat at outdoor snack tables in the morning and in the canteen at lunchtime. All dietary requirements are catered for, with healthy meals provided and themed meals linked to learning. Parents are asked to provide two healthy snacks each day, ensuring all snacks are nut-free and appropriate for safety.
Outdoor learning
The Lyceum makes full use of its location to enhance learning. Reception pupils visit local fire stations, art galleries, parks, and the Lyceum Garden at Spitalfields City Farm, where they grow plants, fruit, and vegetables and care for animals. Visitors from the community, including police officers and professionals linked to class topics, provide workshops and answer children’s questions.
Emotional wellbeing
A calm, happy atmosphere is a hallmark of The Lyceum. In Reception, pupils’ emotional wellbeing is a priority. Each class has a visual feelings chart to allow children to express their emotions, and Circle Time sessions explore all aspects of personal, social, and emotional development. Pupils are guided to develop kindness, resilience, and a growth mindset, supported by a dedicated team at every stage of their learning journey.

Children can also try languages including Spanish, French and Mandarin, along with computing, chess, model building and cooking. There is something for every age and every interest, from our youngest Reception children to Year 6 pupils getting ready for senior school.
Our extracurricular activities in school run before and after the school day as part of our wrap-around care, which is available from 8:00am until 5:45pm. Breakfast Club and morning clubs start the day. A choice of after-school clubs, followed by Late Club or Homework Club, helps busy working families. Most of our pupils choose at least one club each term, and many try several over the year.
Every club has a purpose. Whether a child is landing their first judo throw, learning lines for a drama showcase or perfecting a bake, they are building confidence, resilience and independence that carry straight back into the classroom.
Our Extracurricular Activities
Our clubs programme is designed to broaden horizons, and it changes with the seasons and with our pupils’ interests. Here is a flavour of what’s on offer.
Creative and Performing Arts
Budding artists and performers can explore Arts & Crafts, Oodles of Doodles, Cartoon Club, Art Club and Design Club with Lego. For those who love to perform, there is Drama Club, Ballet, Pom Cheer, Pom Dance, Boogie Beats and Street Dance. These clubs build on our specialist art teaching and the many performance opportunities across the school year.
Sport and Movement
From Mini Movers and Multisports for our youngest pupils to Football, Table Tennis, Fencing and Judo for older children, our sports clubs develop coordination, fitness and team spirit. They complement our curriculum sport programme and our inter-House competitions.
Music and Languages
Music Club and Sing & Sign, which introduces British Sign Language through song, sit alongside our thriving music department, choirs and ensembles. Language lovers can extend their learning with Spanish, French and Mandarin clubs.
STEM and Problem Solving
Curious minds thrive in Lego Club, Model Building Club, Computer Club, Chess Club and Number Mayhem, our early-morning maths club. These clubs build logical thinking, perseverance and creativity, and they extend the hands-on learning pupils enjoy in our STEAM Studio.
Cooking and Life Skills
In Big Cook Little Cook and Ready Set Bake, children learn to follow recipes, measure ingredients and work as a team, with delicious results.
Wellbeing and Quieter Time
Not every child wants to run around at the end of a busy day. Story Time, Film Club and Homework Club offer calmer ways to unwind. Late Club gives our youngest pupils a relaxed, supervised space until pick-up.
Seasonal and Ad Hoc Clubs
Alongside our weekly timetable, we run ad hoc clubs throughout the year. We also introduce new activities each term in response to pupil suggestions, so the programme always feels fresh.

Research summarised in the Education Endowment Foundation’s Teaching and Learning Toolkit shows that activities such as arts participation and physical activity can have a positive effect on pupils’ learning and wellbeing. Frequently Asked Questions
How often are the club timetables updated?
Our club timetables are refreshed every term. This lets us respond to pupil interest, include seasonal activities and introduce new clubs, so the extracurricular programme stays varied and exciting throughout the academic year. We welcome suggestions from pupils and parents, and many of our most popular clubs began as a child’s idea. The latest timetables are always published on this page.
Can my child join more than one extracurricular club?
Yes. We encourage pupils to take part in a range of activities where they can. Trying different clubs helps children explore new interests, develop a wider range of skills and build confidence. Most pupils choose at least one club each term, and many combine a morning club with an after-school activity, subject to availability and timetable compatibility.
Are extracurricular activities included in school fees?
Our extracurricular clubs are charged separately from tuition fees, and costs vary by club. Breakfast Club can also be booked on an ad hoc basis. Current charges for clubs and wrap-around care are set out on our Fees page, and we always tell parents about any costs in advance so families can plan with confidence.
How do parents register their child for extracurricular clubs?
Before each term begins, we share the new club timetables with families, together with details of how to book and the deadline for securing a place. Places are allocated once registrations close, and we confirm your child’s clubs before the new timetable begins. If you have questions about booking or which clubs suit your child, please contact us.
What happens if a club is full?
Our most popular clubs can fill quickly, so we recommend booking early. If a club is full, we will offer a place on the waiting list or suggest a similar activity for your child. We regularly review demand, and when interest is high we look at running additional sessions or introducing a new club the following term.
How do I choose the right club for my child?
Start with your child’s interests, and don’t be afraid to try something new. An energetic child may love Multisports or Fencing, while a creative thinker might enjoy Cartoon Club or Drama. A good mix of active, creative and quieter clubs works well. Our teachers know every child individually and are always happy to suggest clubs that would suit them.

School Curriculum
Across all age ranges, pupils enjoy a diverse and exciting topic-based curriculum.
Our topic-based approach is integrated with the National Curriculum, providing broad and balanced cross curricular opportunities that help to develop a strong work ethic, emphasising independent thinking and learning skills. Children work within broad topics which draw on many subjects, including English, Geography, History and Art.
Where there are strong links, the main topic is taught across the curriculum, but where lessons do not link with the topic, these are taught discretely. This topic-based method inspires the children to fully immerse themselves in the topics and, by providing a holistic approach to education, it enables vital connections to be made so that a pupil’s understanding of the world can be fully developed.

English — Ms Graden
At The Lyceum, we have developed a method of teaching that not only covers the objectives in the National Primary Curriculum but inspires our pupils to develop a life-long love of reading and writing. Children at The Lyceum are empowered to develop their skills and vocabulary in order to write and speak confidently, eloquently and creatively. We teach our pupils using methods that encourage reading for pleasure and allow the children to enjoy a range of genres and texts. Our pupils are given the opportunity to develop their writing, reading, grammar, punctuation, spelling and handwriting skills on a daily basis.
Phonics
Word reading skills are taught using the Letters and Sounds curriculum in the Early Years Phase and throughout KS1. Our phonics lessons provide pupils with the skills to decode words in order to read fluently and to break down words in order to spell confidently. We use games, songs, puppets and many other methods to engage the children in reading and spelling.
Reading
Reading skills and comprehension are taught and practised every day at our school. The children have the opportunity to read as a class, within groups and one to one with their teacher. Each child is given a reading diary in which parents and teachers can communicate about their progress. Children are encouraged to read a wide range of high quality texts which challenge their reading skills and develop their knowledge. We believe that varied and regular reading is the basis for promoting a life-long love of reading, as well as developing interesting and vibrant writing skills.
Writing
As with our approach to teaching reading, our pupils are given opportunities to write about a wide range of subjects and high quality texts. Our lessons allow the children to develop a vast vocabulary which they can draw on to write across a range of genres, for a range of purposes and for a range of readers. The children learn precursive handwriting in Year 1 which gives them the basis to develop fully joined, cursive handwriting as they move through the school. Presentation is very important to us at The Lyceum and we encourage all pupils to take pride in their work.
Spelling
We use the Read Write Inc spelling scheme which follows the Primary National Curriculum and gives the children the opportunity to practise key spellings on a daily basis. During our English lessons, we expose pupils to a wide range of vocabulary so that they are able to use and spell words above and beyond the age expected standard.
Spoken Language
At The Lyceum, we place a great deal of emphasis on ensuring that all our pupils are given a wealth of experiences with which to live out and perform their work. From the Foundation Stage onwards, a rich Speech and Language programme ensures that all pupils are given the necessary skills with which to communicate and articulate their ideas. We incorporate lots of opportunities for pupils to perform; whether it be in class or on stage in productions and class performances.
We also recognise that the knowledge and skills found in our English lessons cross over into many other curriculum subjects. We make the most of these opportunities in order that our pupils can achieve their very best.
Maths — Miss Hardman
The National Curriculum for Mathematics aims to ensure that all pupils become fluent, reason mathematically and can solve problems. We believe that a high quality Mathematics education provides a foundation for understanding the world, the ability to reason mathematically, an appreciation of the beauty and power of mathematics and a sense of enjoyment and curiosity about the subject.
Learn more about how we nurture mathematical thinking:

Through a structured curriculum aligned with the National Curriculum, we develop pupils’ fluency in number facts, arithmetic skills, and problem-solving strategies. Our approach ensures that every child builds resilience, accuracy, and logical reasoning abilities, equipping them with the skills needed for lifelong mathematical success.

How is Maths taught in Years 1-4?
At The Lyceum, we follow the Maths No Problem series because we are committed to ensuring that every child develops an understanding and love of Maths. With the right kind of teaching and support, we can ensure this happens. Maths No Problem uses a mastery teaching approach from Singapore. It is aligned with the 2014 English National Curriculum for Mathematics and was assessed by the DfE’s expert panel, which judged that it met the core criteria for a high-quality textbook to support teaching for mastery. By incorporating established learning research into a highly effective approach, Singapore has become a “laboratory of maths teaching”. The Maths No Problem series is founded on the international research of Piaget, Dienes, Bruner, Skempand and Vygotsky and has been tested and refined over the last 30 years in Singapore. The series follows a spiral approach; this means each time a topic is revisited, we build on prior knowledge by linking new ideas and looking at the concepts in more depth. Each year group is organised in this way meaning that children revisit topics throughout their primary education and continue to build on the knowledge that they already have.
Teaching for Mastery
The series ensures that children learn to think mathematically and that they make connections and generalisations to help them learn.
During each lesson, we prioritise the mastery of conceptual Maths understanding through the use of real life/everyday problems as children explore and investigate. Communication is key as they work alongside peers to reason, explain and justify their thinking using mathematical vocabulary.
Teachers carefully plan open ended, challenging questions which enable our children to make connections and identify patterns and draw conclusions about Mathematical concepts and problem solving. Misconceptions are addressed as they arise, and teachers actively engage children in proving their ideas.
The whole class works through the programme of study at the same pace with ample time on each topic before moving on. Ideas are revisited at higher levels as the curriculum progresses through the years. Tasks and activities are designed to be approachable for all while still containing challenging components. For advanced learners, the textbooks also contain non-routine questions for pupils to develop their higher-order thinking skills. Concepts are taught using problem-solving approaches to encourage pupils’ higher-level thinking. The focus is on working with pupils’ core competencies, building on what they know to develop their relational understanding, based on Richard Skemp’s work. During each lesson, all children use apparatus or visual aid. As they make progress in the lesson, they move towards using abstract representations for Mathematical concepts (The CPA approach).
In addition to these core Maths lessons, all children have focused lessons on times tables, reasoning and arithmetic to provide security and depth to their learning. This allows pupils to make connections between Mathematical topics and ensures we are able to support all children whilst stretching and challenging the highest attainers. Furthermore, pupils are able to develop and refine the skills they will require in Years 5 and 6 when faced with the 11+ exams.
Structure of a Maths No Problem lesson
In Focus
Includes questions related to various lesson objectives as an introductory activity for pupils. Pupils discuss and explore a range of methods to solve the problem. They use journals to record their ideas and are encouraged to describe methods and explain their thinking. These journals provide pupils with opportunities to show their understanding of the Mathematical concepts learnt.
Let’s Learn
This introduces new concepts through a Concrete, Pictorial, Abstract approach with the use of engaging pictures and manipulatives. Guided examples are provided for reinforcement. Teachers reinforce non-negotiable learning objectives through direct teaching.
Guided Practice
This comprises of questions for further consolidation and for the immediate evaluation of pupils’ learning. Children complete tasks either independently, with a peer or collectively as a class. Discussion follows to encourage reasoning and mathematical fluency to be shown.
Workbooks
Pupils independently answer a range of questions directly related to the National Curriculum learning objective. These are arranged in a non-uniform way to allow for children to evidence their mastery of the Mathematical concept being taught.
Year 5 and 6 Maths Curriculum
In line with The Lyceum School’s curriculum policy (2a) which outlines the need to cover both the National Curriculum and the syllabus required for independent schools’ entrance exams, a greater level of importance is placed on the 11+ process in Upper Key Stage 2. Whilst still covering all areas of the National Curriculum, Maths lessons in Year 5 and 6 prepare the children for greater depth and potential difficulty of Mathematical knowledge required.

Times tables at The Lyceum
At The Lyceum, we believe that having a secure knowledge of times tables is incredibly important for children and regular practice of tables is one of the most valuable ways parents can support children in their learning. To achieve well in Maths throughout school, children need to be able to recall any times tables (up to 12x) and answer within two or three seconds. This leaves no time for counting up to the answer from 2x, 3x, 4x etc. and is called ‘fluency’. Alongside focused weekly times table lessons, there are a range of tools we use to boost fluency, such as Times Table Rock Stars.
Science — Mr Biles
At The Lyceum School, we recognise the importance of Science in every aspect of daily life. Our aim is to equip our children with the key working scientifically skills, knowledge and vocabulary motivated by our core skills of active learning, basic skills and creative thinking.
Our Science curriculum is shaped by the National Curriculum for Science, our school values and the ethos at The Lyceum. Our Science curriculum aims to ensure that all children:
We plan for ‘working scientifically’ skills to be built-on and developed throughout a child’s time at the school so that they can make connections in their learning and become thinkers and investigators. This will enable them to apply their knowledge of Science when using equipment, conducting experiments, building arguments and explaining concepts confidently. We aim to plan and provide opportunities for critical evaluation of evidence, to be reflective, responsible and to ask questions.
Across the school, continuous progression is at the heart of our curriculum design. Science lessons are planned to be a part of the concept-based enquiry questions, where possible these are made cross-curricular. Children are given the opportunity to use a variety of data, such as statistics, pictures and photographs. ICT, reading, writing, speaking and listening are strongly developed through Science. Where meaningful links are not possible, Science is taught as a discrete subject to ensure the quality and integrity of the core subject can be upheld. The structure of Science lessons allows for the incremental acquisition of skills and knowledge and time to address misconceptions. There is a strong focus on providing children with opportunities to apply their knowledge.
Assessment is on-going throughout the learning process and includes observing children at work, questioning, class discussions, quizzes, written and verbal feedback, practical sessions to apply knowledge and skills, and independent learning in books.

Reception Curriculum
Teaching staff are on hand each day at drop-off time to greet the Reception classes and their parents; this ensures a smooth transition into school as any messages from home can be passed straight onto the team. Collection time also gives you a chance to catch up with the teaching staff, and if you feel you need more time to chat, you can always ask to arrange a ‘touch base’ meeting with them at any time. We understand that starting ‘big school’ can at first be quite an emotional experience, both for you and your child, and we will be on hand to reassure and provide comfort when it is needed.
Very swiftly, you will find that your child has settled into the new routines and is coming into school happily. Once they are, we would ask you to help them to develop their independent skills. Reception children, for instance, are encouraged to take ownership of their belongings. They are expected to carry their own school bags into class and soon learn to unpack them and hang up their coats and hats. Gradually they learn what to bring in each day, such as their homework pack or their musical instrument, and they remember when to wear their PE Kit or full uniform.
Child-Initiated Play
Play-based education is at the heart of all we do and, although the children are learning at a very swift rate, they are not aware that they are doing so. Imaginative and creative lessons ensure key skills are gained but without any sense of pressure. When learning is enjoyable, a natural thirst for it is developed; there is not the usual separation between work and play.
In Reception, children have a slightly more structured day than they would have had in Nursery. They have three morning lessons, with a play/snack after lesson one. These are followed by lunch and playtime. In the afternoon there will be a topic-based lesson and structured play, or a park visit. The curriculum is enriched with weekly STEAM, Spanish, Music, PE/Dance and Yoga lessons.
Our dedicated team quickly learn about the interests and needs of each individual child and they cater for their next steps accordingly. We do not formally group or label children, but we do provide a subtly differentiated curriculum, extending children as and when they are ready for a challenge.
Literacy encompasses the skills needed to communicate and understand ideas through reading and writing. In Reception, we generally refer to this area of the curriculum as ‘Phonics’. Phonics is a systematic approach to teaching early reading skills and simply means matching letter symbols to their corresponding sounds.
Initially, children are taught the most common sound made by alphabetic letters on their own. Rather than teaching from a-z, letter sounds are introduced in an order which allows children to combine them and begin to explore and read short words. For example, the first six letters and sounds in our Phonics scheme are s,a,t,p,i,n. We then explore what happens when some of these letters join to form words, of which there are 106! The most commonly used letters in short words are then drip fed until children have a basic understanding of the phonetic alphabet.
When ready, children are then introduced to the language and understanding of di/trigraphs. Digraphs are when two letters join together and make a new sound e.g. ch, sh, oa. Trigraphs are when three letters join together to make a new sound e.g. igh.
In Reception, we encourage children to write using the sounds they know. Phonics lessons continue across Key Stage 1, allowing children to understand and learn spelling rules for more complex words.
Alongside our Phonics Scheme, we do introduce “tricky words” which are the most common unphonetic words in our vocabulary. These are taught discretely to ensure children can access reading books and use them in their own writing. This includes words such as “the” and “was”.
Workshops for parents are provided in both Phonics, early Maths and Parenting, and support is provided to parents regularly throughout the year to help you better understand the teaching of Phonics and how to support your child as they begin to read and write.
We pride ourselves in the fact that our pupils enjoy Numeracy at The Lyceum. By the end of Reception, children are not only able to find answers, but they can explain their process and prove their logic. We steadily build across the year from number recognition to addition, subtraction, halving, doubling and solving problems. We embed correct mathematical language from the beginning and ensure children are aware of mathematics in the wider world, preparing them for “White Rose Maths” which is introduced from Year One. We also focus on shape, position and movement, time and measurement.
Snack and lunchtime are both supervised by members of the EYFS team and we closely monitor the eating habits of all children to ensure that they have a balanced diet. At snack-time, the children eat at our outdoor snack tables after their morning play. At lunchtime, all children eat in our lovely canteen and individual dietary requirements/allergies are catered for. Children are provided with a range of healthy meals and regularly enjoyed themed meals in relation to their learning.
EYFS children need to come to school with two healthy snack portions, one for the morning and one for the afternoon. Fruit is encouraged for the morning snack. We ask that grapes are cut in half for safety reasons. We suggest afternoon snacks to be cheese and crackers or rice cakes etc. Sweets/chocolate/crisps are not permitted and all snacks must be completely nut free.
In Reception we regularly use the fantastic location of the school to enhance our learning, by going on trips which are walking distance to the school such as the local fire station, theatres and parks.
We also have our very own “Lyceum Garden” at Spitalfields City Farm, where we grow our own plants, fruit and vegetables and help take care of the animals. We have regular visitors to the school who lead workshops and answer questions from the children, such as local police officers and adults in industries linked to our class topics.
As a school, we are proud of our calm, happy atmosphere which is felt by all as they enter the building. In EYFS, ensuring children are kind, happy, and feel safe is at the heart of everything we do. We ensure all children are given the chance to share how they are feeling at the beginning of each day, and each class has a ‘visual feelings chart’ on the wall to allow children to indicate how they are feeling throughout the day. Regular Circle Time lessons take place, exploring all aspects of personal, social and emotional development (PSED) and assemblies also often link to wellbeing. Children are supported by the dedicated team to navigate any emotional obstacles they face and are encouraged to have a ‘growth mindset’ when it comes to problem solving.

Art
Art & Design at The Lyceum
Art is at the heart of our creative curriculum. At The Lyceum, we believe that art and design stimulate children’s creativity and imagination, giving them visual, tactile and sensory experiences that help them understand and respond to the world around them. Whether they are sketching botanical specimens, sculpting in 3D or painting a scene inspired by another culture, our pupils learn to see closely, think creatively and express themselves with confidence.
Our Approach to Art
Art at our prep school is taught in our specialist art studio and is closely linked to the topics children study across the curriculum. Pupils:
Art Linked to Learning
Our topic-based curriculum means art is never taught in isolation. Projects connect to what pupils are learning in history, geography, science and PSHE, as well as to themes such as Black History Month, Remembrance and diversity. Recent projects have included:
Art is also the “A” in STEAM. In our STEAM studio, “The Owlery”, pupils combine art with science, technology and engineering, designing mechanical automaton toys and creating geometric art with code.
London as Our Gallery
Few prep schools can match our access to world-class art. Our central London location puts some of the greatest museums and galleries in the world within easy reach. Pupils visit exhibitions regularly, take part in gallery workshops and welcome visiting artists into school, seeing great art up close and meeting the people who make it. Find out more about our school trips.
Art Week and Exhibitions
Every year, our whole school comes together for Art Week. Each class researches an artist, movement or theme, and the week ends with collaborative whole-school pieces that fill our corridors with colour. Our pupils’ work has also been recognised beyond school: our collaborative piece A View into The Lyceum was Highly Commended in the Independent Schools Association (ISA) Art Competition.
Budding artists can take their creativity further in our extracurricular clubs, including Art Club, Arts & Crafts, Cartoon Club, Oodles of Doodles and Design Club with Lego.
Why Art Matters
Art develops much more than artistic skill. It builds observation, patience, problem-solving and the confidence to share original ideas, all qualities that support learning across the curriculum. Research summarised by the Education Endowment Foundation suggests that arts participation can have a positive effect on pupils’ wider attainment. Above all, art gives every child a way to express who they are.
Discover more about our Prep School curriculum and our creative approach to learning.
Explore Admissions →
Frequently Asked Questions
How is art taught at The Lyceum?
Art is taught in our specialist art studio as part of a broad, topic-based curriculum. Pupils explore drawing, painting, printmaking, collage and 3D work, study artists from different cultures and periods, and learn to evaluate their own work and that of others. Projects link to class topics, so art deepens learning in history, science and beyond.
Do pupils visit galleries and museums?
Yes. Our central London location gives pupils easy access to world-class museums and galleries, and visits are a regular part of school life. Pupils take part in gallery workshops and exhibitions, and we also welcome visiting artists into school, so children can experience great art first-hand and be inspired by it.
Are there art clubs after school?
Yes. Our extracurricular programme includes several creative clubs, such as Art Club, Arts & Crafts, Cartoon Club, Oodles of Doodles and Design Club with Lego, with options for different year groups. Timetables are refreshed every term, and you’ll find the latest clubs on our Extra Curricular page. New clubs are often added in response to pupils’ ideas.

Special Educational Needs and Disabilities
At The Lyceum, we believe in providing an inclusive, supportive, and tailored educational experience for all our pupils, including those with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). Our commitment to embracing diversity and promoting equality ensures that every child is valued, understood, and provided with the opportunities to thrive both academically and personally.
We recognise the fact that children’s brains develop in different ways – often referred to as neurodiversity – and we actively celebrate and embrace the differences, interests, strengths, and needs of each child as an individual.
Our approach encompasses a number of key areas:
Understanding Each Child
Our approach begins with understanding the unique profile of each child. Through careful observation, assessment, and collaboration with parents, we identify the specific needs and strengths of our SEND pupils. This holistic understanding informs every aspect of our support strategy, ensuring it is as individualised and effective as possible.
Tailored Support Strategies
We develop tailored support strategies that align with each child’s unique needs, focusing on creating an accessible, engaging, and nurturing learning environment. Our strategies may include:
Personalised Learning Plans: these plans outline specific goals, accommodations, and interventions tailored to the child’s needs.
Inclusive Teaching Practices: Our teachers, under the guidance of Mrs Machado, focus on inclusive education strategies, aiming for all children to access the curriculum and participate fully in classroom activities.
Specialist Support: Mrs Machado provides targeted support and where necessary, we also collaborate with external specialists such as speech and language therapists, occupational therapists, and educational psychologists.
Assistive Resources: We utilise a range of assistive resources to support learning and independence.
Building Skills and Confidence
Beyond academic achievement, we focus on building social, emotional, and life skills. Our nurturing environment encourages SEND pupils to develop confidence, resilience, and a positive self-image. We offer a range of extracurricular activities and school-wide initiatives that foster inclusivity, friendship, and community spirit.
Collaboration with Families
We believe that a strong partnership between school and home is vital. Regular communication with families ensures that parents are fully informed and involved in their child’s education. We welcome feedback and collaboration from parents and strive to work together to support our pupils’ learning and well-being.
Training and Awareness
To foster an inclusive school culture, we provide ongoing training for all our staff on SEND awareness, strategies, and interventions. This commitment to professional development ensures our team is equipped to meet the diverse needs of our pupils.
Commitment to Continuous Improvement
We are committed to continuously improving our SEND provision. Through regular review and reflection, we seek to adapt and enhance our strategies, resources, and practices to meet the evolving needs of our pupils.
At The Lyceum, we are dedicated to ensuring that every child, regardless of their individual needs, is given the support, encouragement, and opportunities to achieve their full potential. Our approach to SEND reflects our wider ethos of respect, inclusion, and the belief in the limitless potential of every child.

Mrs Machado
Mrs Machado
Mrs Machado is a specialist teacher with over 20 years’ classroom experience and has worked extensively to deliver lessons that are fun and engaging for pupils with a range of educational needs. Her speciality is creating personalised learning for learners to support them to achieve their full potential, whatever their needs.
In addition to her teaching qualifications, Clare holds a BSc in Psychology and a MA in Specific Learning Difficulties (dyslexia). She is accredited by the British Dyslexia Association and is qualified to administer full diagnostic dyslexia assessments.
